findings.asked: Set up and solve a quadratic from the area of a trapezium.
findings.wentWrong: Most scored zero: the shape was treated as a rectangle, or the height expression could not be formed when the trapezium was split. Those who started correctly usually finished, choosing the positive root and substituting back.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Named the shape, wrote the trapezium area formula with every length as a bracketed expression, expanded, solved, and checked the lengths.
findings.rule: Identify the shape and its formula before writing any algebra.

findings.asked: Show that a quadratic follows from a right-angled triangle, then solve it.
findings.wentWrong: Many wrote an area equation (x times (34 - x) = 240) instead of using Pythagoras and got nothing. Expanding the squared bracket was error-prone. In the solving part, factorising produced wrong roots (40 and 6) and the formula was misused.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote Pythagoras with the bracketed side, expanded (a - b) squared correctly, and used the formula with care.
findings.rule: (a - b) squared has a middle term; check the expansion before simplifying.

findings.asked: Set up and solve a quadratic from the areas of a square and a trapezium.
findings.wentWrong: The hardest question on the paper (one in twenty). Most stated one area and stopped; a few scaled the square's area by 1.5; expansion errors were common; some solvers did not check both roots against the lengths.
findings.rule: After solving, substitute each root back into the length expressions and reject any that fail.

findings.asked: Show that a quadratic equation follows from a triangle's area, then solve it to find lengths.
findings.wentWrong: Three groups: fully correct; blank or just solved the given equation; or started but lost the half in the area formula. In (b) most scored nothing, though some solved the equation without having done (a).
findings.rule: Area of a triangle is half base times height - the half must appear in the setup.

findings.asked: Find the radius of a cone by setting up an equation from a difference of two volumes.
findings.wentWrong: Two per cent got full marks, nearly three fifths got zero. Those who set up the subtraction usually squared 3r without brackets, and then could not simplify the terms.
findings.rule: (3r) squared = 9r squared - bracket a product before squaring.

findings.asked: Show that a right-angled triangle's area gives a stated quadratic; then solve it and use trigonometry.
findings.wentWrong: Marks were all or nothing. Many tried to bend their working towards the printed equation, or simply solved it; some used 4x where x + 4 was meant. Part (b) went better: most solved the quadratic and knew to use tan.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Started from the diagram, wrote area = half x (x)(x + 4) = given value, and expanded to reach the printed form line by line.
findings.rule: In a 'show that', start from the diagram and arrive at the printed equation - never start from it.

findings.asked: Set up and solve a quadratic from the area of an L-shaped compound rectangle.
findings.wentWrong: Most added the four given lengths' rectangles without noticing the overlap and lost all five marks; some found the compound area but never used the stated total of 122. A few left the negative root on the answer line.
findings.rule: Split a compound shape so no region is counted twice, and set the expression equal to the area given.

ruleToRemember: Write the geometric fact in words (area, Pythagoras, volume), then in algebra with every length bracketed; expand carefully; a 'show that' derives the printed equation; after solving, check which root gives sensible lengths.
aStarSignal: Setting up a quadratic from an unfamiliar figure (overlapping shapes, a cone difference) without scaffolding, with correct bracket handling throughout.
